evals.prompt: I have demand data for 572 UK grocery stores at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/basics/demand_uk.parquet. My boss says we'll only enter this market if monthly demand per store is above 1750 units. Can you walk me through how to check this? I'm new to hypothesis testing.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: asks for/uses the absolute path, calls scripts/load_data.py (or its Python equivalent) to load the parquet, finds and reads demand_uk_description.md to learn that demand is total category sales in units per store per month, picks alt_hyp='greater' from the business decision (and explicitly explains why one-sided is appropriate here — entry decision only triggers when demand exceeds threshold), fits with rsm.basics.single_mean({'demand_uk': df}, var='demand', alt_hyp='greater', conf=0.95, comp_value=1750), prints summary(), then explains: H0 (mean = 1750) and Ha (mean > 1750) in plain English, sample stats (mean ≈ 1953, n=572, sd ≈ 815), the three equivalent verdicts (p < .001 → reject; one-sided 95% lower bound 1897 > 1750 → reject; observed t ≈ 5.97 ≫ critical t ≈ 1.65 → reject), reports the effect size 'diff ≈ 203 units above threshold' in units (not just p < .001), and concludes that management should enter the market.

evals.prompt: Same data at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/basics/demand_uk.parquet, but my prof wants me to also do a two-sided test of 'is the demand different from 1750?' at the 99% confidence level. How does the answer change?
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: refits with rsm.basics.single_mean({'demand_uk': df}, var='demand', alt_hyp='two-sided', conf=0.99, comp_value=1750), shows the new summary, explicitly explains how the output changes versus the one-sided 95% case: (a) the p-value is now the two-sided p (still < .001), (b) the CI is now a two-sided interval (roughly [1865, 2041]) — both bounds finite rather than [lo, +inf) — and is wider than the original because 99% confidence is stricter than 95% AND two-sided spends alpha in both tails, (c) the critical t for a two-sided test at α=0.01 is approximately ±2.58 from prob_calc('tdist', df=571, pub=0.995), not ±1.65, (d) the verdict is still 'reject H0' but the substantive interpretation is now 'demand differs from 1750 in either direction' rather than 'demand exceeds 1750'. Discusses the power tradeoff briefly: two-sided is less powerful than one-sided at the same alpha, and 99% confidence is stricter than 95%. Mentions that you typically don't pick one-sided vs two-sided or 95% vs 99% based on which gives the answer you want — those are choices set by the question, not by the data.

evals.prompt: Test whether demand differs from 1750 in this dataset: ~/Downloads/demand.parquet . Use a 95% CI.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: notices the path is not absolute (uses ~), asks the user for the absolute path before running anything else, does NOT silently expand the tilde or guess. (We use this case to verify the skill enforces the absolute-path requirement from Step 1 of SKILL.md.)

evals.prompt: I ran a single-mean test on demand at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/basics/demand_uk.parquet, but using comp_value=1900 and alt_hyp='two-sided'. The p-value came out as 0.118, well above 0.05. So the mean isn't different from 1900, right? Let me write that up and move on.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: (1) pushes back on 'fail-to-reject = no difference' framing — 'fail to reject H0' is not 'accept H0'; (2) reruns or re-reads the summary and explicitly reports both the diff (sample mean 1953 vs comp_value 1900 → diff ≈ 53 units) and the 95% CI (roughly [1886, 2020]); (3) notes that the CI includes 1900 (consistent with fail-to-reject) but also includes values up to ~2020, so the data are equally consistent with a 'true mean = 2020' world; (4) explicitly explains why the p = 0.118 vs p = 0.04 framing is a cliff: p = 0.118 is moderate evidence against H0, not 'no evidence', and the threshold is a convention; (5) leads with the confidence interval as the more informative output and reframes the conclusion as 'the data are consistent with a population mean anywhere from about 1886 to 2020 units; 1900 is one of those plausible values, but so are values quite a bit higher'; (6) does NOT just say 'p > 0.05, the mean equals 1900' and stop; (7) optionally suggests checking effect size in business terms — is a ~3% difference (53/1900) meaningful for the decision being made?
